before: Running language models on local hardware requires sufficient memory for both the weights and the computations performed during inference. Representing weights at lower precision reduces their storage requirements. Whether the resulting model preserves the grammatical distinctions made by its reference counterpart is a separate empirical question. Multilingual evaluations have shown that the effects of quantization vary across languages and tasks and that automatic metrics can underestimate the degradation observed by human evaluators (Marchisio et al., 2024).
after: Running language models on local hardware requires sufficient memory for both the weights and the computations performed during inference. Low-precision methods can reduce inference memory requirements, but their numerical designs differ. LLM.int8() combines 8-bit multiplication with a higher-precision path for outlier features, whereas SmoothQuant transforms weights and activations to support W8A8 inference (Dettmers et al., 2022; Xiao et al., 2023). These efficiency results motivate a separate empirical question: whether quantization preserves a model’s preferences on specific grammatical contrasts.

before: In Turkish, grammatical relations such as agreement, case selection, and subordination are often expressed through morphology. A single word can contain several morphemes, while a language model’s tokenizer can place boundaries that do not coincide with morpheme boundaries. Sentence length and the distribution of morphemes can therefore affect the interpretation of minimal-pair scores (Başar & Bisazza, 2026). A decline in accuracy alone does not establish which grammatical distinction has become harder to recognize.
after: In Turkish, grammatical relations such as agreement, case selection, and subordination are often expressed through morphology. Tokenization is therefore relevant to how linguistic information is presented to a model. Toraman et al. (2023) compared five tokenization approaches, including a morphological-level tokenizer, in Turkish language models evaluated on six downstream tasks. Their study motivates attention to tokenization choices, but it does not establish how a fixed tokenizer interacts with weight quantization in minimal-pair judgments. A decline in accuracy alone does not identify the grammatical or representational cause.

before: Quantization schemes with the same nominal bit width can implement different numerical operations. LLM.int8() retains a higher-precision computation path for outlier features while using 8-bit matrix multiplication for most values (Dettmers et al., 2022). GPTQ uses approximate second-order information for post-training weight quantization (Frantar et al., 2023). AWQ uses activation statistics to identify scaling factors that protect salient weights (Lin et al., 2024). SmoothQuant redistributes quantization difficulty between activations and weights to support 8-bit computation for both (Xiao et al., 2023). The present comparison holds the MLX affine scheme and group size fixed and varies the weight bit width. No further training or task-specific fine-tuning was performed.
after: Quantization schemes with the same nominal bit width can implement different numerical operations. LLM.int8() uses vector-wise quantization for most features and a 16-bit computation path for outlier dimensions (Dettmers et al., 2022). SmoothQuant uses a mathematically equivalent transformation to shift quantization difficulty from activations to weights, enabling 8-bit quantization of both (Xiao et al., 2023). These methods illustrate why bit width alone does not specify a quantization procedure. The present comparison holds the MLX affine scheme and group size fixed and varies the weight bit width. No further training or task-specific fine-tuning was performed.

before: Marchisio et al. found that quantization affected languages differently across multilingual models (Marchisio et al., 2024). Their results motivate language-specific evaluation but do not establish a ranking of Turkish relative to other languages. Bayram et al. examined quantization in Turkish classification and summarization tasks alongside system efficiency (Bayram et al., 2025). Our outcome differs from those task scores: we track whether a model changes its preference between two sentences and whether each change agrees with the benchmark label. Differences in tasks and scoring preclude a direct ranking across the studies.
after: Published efficiency gains depend on the evaluated model, numerical method, and workload. Dettmers et al. (2022) report memory savings for mixed-precision 8-bit inference, while Xiao et al. (2023) evaluate memory and speed for W8A8 inference. Neither result establishes preservation of Turkish morphosyntactic preferences under MLX affine weight quantization. For Turkish, Toraman et al. (2023) show that tokenization granularity and vocabulary size warrant empirical evaluation across downstream tasks. Our study connects these concerns by measuring grammatical preferences and local resource use while holding the tokenizer fixed. Differences in tasks and quantization procedures preclude direct numerical rankings across these studies.

before: BLiMP uses minimally contrasting sentences to probe language models’ sensitivity to grammatical distinctions (Warstadt et al., 2020). TurBLiMP extends this approach to 16 Turkish linguistic phenomena, including constructions involving flexible word order and morphological subordination (Başar et al., 2025). Başar and Bisazza investigated how morpheme counts, subword counts, length, and tokenizer alignment with morphological boundaries affect such evaluations (Başar & Bisazza, 2026). We treat minimal-pair accuracy as a measure of sensitivity to the selected contrasts. Our token-to-word ratio is a sentence-level proxy for fragmentation and does not measure morpheme counts.
after: BLiMP uses minimally contrasting sentences to probe language models’ sensitivity to grammatical distinctions in English (Warstadt et al., 2020). TurBLiMP provides the Turkish minimal pairs used in the present experiment (Başar et al., 2025). Turkish tokenization research compares character-, subword-, word-, and morphology-related representations, with evaluations on downstream tasks rather than the quantized minimal-pair task studied here (Toraman et al., 2023). We treat minimal-pair accuracy as sensitivity to the selected contrasts. Our token-to-word ratio is a sentence-level fragmentation proxy; it does not identify morphemes or measure alignment with gold morphological boundaries.

before: The fragmentation results complement morphology-aware evaluations (Başar & Bisazza, 2026). A word split into several tokens need not represent a difficult grammatical contrast. Punctuation contributes to the numerator of the proxy, and length enters both the ratio and the adjustment model. The token-length sensitivity interval includes the neutral value, which limits any interpretation of the negative slope as a robust linguistic effect.
after: The fragmentation analysis addresses a different question from comparisons of alternative Turkish tokenizers (Toraman et al., 2023): here, the tokenizer is fixed and only weight precision changes. A word split into several tokens need not represent a difficult grammatical contrast. Punctuation contributes to the numerator of the proxy, and length enters both the ratio and the adjustment model. The token-length sensitivity interval includes the neutral value, which limits any interpretation of the negative slope as a robust linguistic effect.
